items.title: Which EF Core version check the guide warns against
items.body:
The guide's warning is direct: "Do **not** read the row, compare the version in C#, and then write it - that is a check-then-act race that two requests can both pass." Two requests can both read version 4, both see "4 matches", and both write. Instead, the database must do the comparison in the same statement as the write: put `Version == expected` in the UPDATE's WHERE clause and count the rows changed. Zero rows means the check failed.

Why the other options are not what it warns against:
- A concurrency token makes EF add the version to the WHERE clause; that is database-enforced.
- A version comparison in the UPDATE's WHERE is the recommended form.
- Mapping EF's concurrency exception to 412 reports the database's own check correctly.

excerpts.quote: **The version check becomes a `WHERE` clause.** This is the part most worth learning. Do **not** read the row, compare the version in C#, and then write it - that is a check-then-act race that two requests can both pass. Make the database do the comparison and count the rows it changed:

var affected = await db.Pastes .Where(p => p.Slug == slug && p.Version == expectedVersion) // the If-Match value .ExecuteUpdateAsync(setters => setters .SetProperty(p => p.Content, command.Content) .SetProperty(p => p.Title, command.Title) .SetProperty(p => p.Visibility, command.Visibility) .SetProperty(p => p.Version, p => p.Version + 1), cancellationToken);

items.title: What a retry with the same request ID gets
items.body:
When the server accepts a create, it stores a **receipt** keyed by the request ID. If the response is lost and the browser retries with the same ID, the same exact body and the same key, the server finds that receipt and returns the paste it already created. It does not write another revision. That makes the create **idempotent**: doing it twice has the effect of doing it once. The concepts chapter lists the other cases: a changed body under the same ID is a conflict (409), and a deleted or expired result is gone (410), never recreated. Only a *new* request ID can create a second paste.

Why the others are wrong:
- 409 is for the same ID with a *different* body; this retry is identical.
- 410 is for a paste that was deleted or has expired; nothing timed out here.
- A second paste only comes from a new request ID.

excerpts.quote: A retry with the same ID, exact body and key finds the accepted receipt. The response identifies the existing paste and does not write another workspace revision.
if (existing is null || existing.IsExpired(now)) throw new PasteRuleException("This creation request was already accepted, but its paste is deleted or expired. It was not created again.", 410);

items.title: Which rotation fix the guide rejects, and why
items.body:
Rotation has an "acknowledgement gap". The server makes the old key invalid and the response is lost. Now the client only has the old key, which no longer works, so it cannot retry. The guide offers two real fixes: a **durable rotation receipt** keyed by an operation ID and bound to both key hashes, with a defined replay response; or a carefully designed **proof using the new key**. Either needs limits, rejection behaviour and tests. What it rejects outright: "Do not solve the problem by accepting both keys forever; that defeats rotation." The point of rotating is that the old key stops working.

Why the other options are not the rejected one:
- A proof using the new capability is one of the two approaches it suggests.
- Limits and a replay response are required parts of either approach.
- A durable rotation receipt is the other suggested approach.

excerpts.quote: For key rotation, identify an acknowledgement gap before writing the endpoint. Suppose the old key becomes invalid and the success response disappears. Retrying with only the old key cannot authenticate an ordinary second rotation. One approach is a durable rotation receipt keyed by an operation ID and bound to the old and new key hashes, with an explicitly defined replay response. Another is a carefully designed proof using the new capability. Either approach needs limits, rejection behavior and tests. Do not solve the problem by accepting both keys forever; that defeats rotation.

items.title: Why Tab B gets 412 and must keep its text
items.body:
Both tabs started from version 4. Tab A saves first with `If-Match: "4"`, so the server stores "alpha" as version 5. Tab B also says `If-Match: "4"`, but the current version is now 5. The precondition fails, the server answers **412** and changes nothing: version 5 stays. On the client, Tab B's text "beta" must be kept so the user can review it. It must not swap in 5 and resend, because that would overwrite "alpha" without anyone seeing it. The concepts chapter: "The expected version belongs to the draft, while the latest saved version belongs to the current server representation."

Why the others are wrong:
- Arriving later does not win; the version check rejects it.
- There is no merging.
- Automatically resending with version 5 is exactly what the guide forbids.

excerpts.quote: Tab A sends If-Match: "4" and content "alpha". Server stores version 5 and returns it. Tab B sends If-Match: "4" and content "beta". Server returns 412; version 5 remains unchanged.
The client must keep Tab B's text. It should not silently replace `4` with `5` and retry, because that would overwrite `alpha` without review.

items.title: Concept: Goal/Check tickets and the status codes they assert
items.body:
05-PRACTICE.md has five tickets in increasing difficulty: page size, key rotation, archival, a move to SQLite, and accounts. Each ends with a **Goal** (what must be true after your change) and a **Check** (the concrete test or command that proves it). A good Check exercises exactly the code the Goal is about, and would fail if the Goal were not met. Checks often name an existing test to copy or keep green.

The Checks assert HTTP status codes, so learn what each means here:

- **400**: the request itself breaks a rule (for example a bad page size).
- **404**: not found, also used so that a wrong key reveals nothing.
- **409**: a conflict with something already accepted.
- **410**: gone; the thing existed but was deleted or expired.
- **412**: precondition failed; the `If-Match` version is no longer current.
- **428**: precondition required; no version was sent at all.

When a quiz gives a Goal and four Checks, match the ticket first: which feature does each Check touch?

excerpts.quote: # Five practice tickets in increasing difficulty
Each ticket should include a short design note, a working UI where relevant, tests at the affected boundaries

readMore.why: All five tickets with their Goals and Checks.
How to run the test tiers.

items.title: Why GET stopped counting views
items.body:
The store keeps everything in one workspace file and rewrites the whole file for every change. The original view counter was a change, so every time someone *read* a paste, the app rewrote the entire file. That turns reads into writes, with all the failure and locking risk of writes. The guide's rule: "Read requests should not unexpectedly perform business writes." The revised app keeps old counts as historical data but no longer increments them on GET, so a failed read is easier to reason about.

Why the others are wrong:
- The 2,000 limit is a cap on stored pastes, not a counter overflow.
- The guide does not mention leaking unlisted pastes as the reason.
- The guide's reason is the rewrite, not a rule about leases on GET.

excerpts.quote: Read requests should not unexpectedly perform business writes. The original view counter caused reading a paste to rewrite the whole file. The revised application retains migrated view counts as historical metadata but does not increment them on GET.
The store loads and rewrites the aggregate for each accepted mutation.

items.title: Goal "ownership enforced on the server": which check fits
items.body:
Ticket 5 introduces accounts, and the Goal is that ownership is enforced *on the server* for every operation in your permission table. The matching Check tries to break it directly: for each write and each non-public read, a test sends user A's valid slug with user B's session and asserts the denial status. The suggested status is 404, consistent with the wrong-key test, so outsiders learn nothing. It ends with an important rule: "A UI test that hides a button does not count." Hiding a button in the browser proves nothing about what the server allows.

Why the other Checks do not fit:
- the pageSize query-string Check belongs to Ticket 1 (choose a page size).
- the run-PasteCommandTests-against-SQLite Check belongs to Ticket 4 (move the store to SQLite).
- the archive-then-repeat-create Check (assert 410) belongs to Ticket 3 (archival).
None of them involves two users.

excerpts.quote: for each write and each non-public read, one test submits user A's valid slug with user B's session and asserts the denial status you chose.
**Ticket 5: introduce accounts and ownership.** Write a design first.

items.title: Concept: who may change it, which version, and what if it is retried
items.body:
02-CONCEPTS.md keeps several questions apart that beginners often mix up. For every write in this app, ask each one separately:

- **Who may do this?** Here the answer is a capability: an edit key. Holding the key grants one action on one paste. It is not a login or a user identity.
- **Is the writer's copy current?** Each paste has a version number. A write says which version it was based on (in an `If-Match` header), and the server compares.
- **What if the same request arrives twice?** A network can lose a response after the server has already acted. A request ID lets the server recognise a repeat.
- **Can the file survive a failed write?** The store writes the whole workspace file, so how it replaces the file matters.

Each question has its own mechanism in the code, and fixing one does not fix the others. When a quiz describes a failure, first decide which of these questions it is really about. Then look up that section of 02-CONCEPTS.md.

excerpts.quote: An edit key is a capability: possession grants a specific action on a specific paste. It is not a username, a login session or proof of personal identity.
Idempotency answers a different question from authorization.

readMore.why: The worked change on stale edits.

items.title: Why changing page size also sets page to 1, and where total comes from
items.body:
If you are on page 3 with 12 per page and switch to 24 per page, "page 3" now means a different range, and may not exist at all. So the event updates both together: `setCriteria((current) => ({ ...current, pageSize: nextSize, page: 1 }))`. For `total`, the guide says to keep it "tied to the same query and language filter", meaning the number the server counted for this exact query. If you computed it from the rows currently on screen, you would only ever see one page's worth, and the next-page button would be wrong.

Why the others are wrong:
- The reason is correctness, not saving a render; and counting on-screen rows is the mistake the guide names.
- The server does not ignore page; the client resets it on purpose.
- React does not require both fields; and total must match the current query, not an old response.

excerpts.quote: setCriteria((current) => ({ ...current, pageSize: nextSize, page: 1 }));
Keep the response's `total` tied to the same query and language filter. If you compute the total from the currently displayed rows, the next-page button will be wrong.

items.title: Why a plain SHA-256 is acceptable for new edit keys
items.body:
Passwords need slow, salted hashes because people pick guessable passwords: an attacker who steals the hashes can try millions of likely guesses quickly. A new edit key is not chosen by a person. The browser generates **32 random bytes**, an enormous number of possibilities. Even with a fast hash, guessing that value by brute force is impractical. The guide: "Because newly generated keys have high entropy, this is different from storing a human password using a fast hash." It also warns that old, user-chosen keys keep their old (weaker) strength.

Why the others are wrong:
- Fixed-time comparison protects the live comparison from timing attacks; it does nothing against offline guessing of a stolen hash.
- The guide says encoding "does not strengthen" keys.
- SHA-256 is a fast general hash, not a slow salted password hash.

excerpts.quote: The application generates 32 random bytes in the browser and sends their base64url representation in a header. The server stores a SHA-256 hash and compares supplied keys using a fixed-time comparison. Because newly generated keys have high entropy, this is different from storing a human password using a fast hash.

items.title: How the sketch tells 404 from 412 when no row was updated
items.body:
The update runs `WHERE Slug == slug && Version == expected`. If it changes 0 rows, there are two possible reasons: no paste has that slug, or one exists but someone already moved its version on. The comment in the sketch says exactly this. So the sketch re-reads the paste without tracking. If it is missing, 404 "Paste was not found."; if it exists, 412 "The paste changed since you loaded it." That gives a precise answer "rather than a vague 409".

Why the others are wrong:
- Zero rows does not always mean stale; the slug may not exist.
- Retrying with the current version would overwrite someone else's change.
- The cause *can* be known by re-reading, so a vague 409 is avoided.

excerpts.quote: if (affected == 0) { // Zero rows means either "no such slug" or "somebody else already advanced the version". // Re-read to tell those apart, so you can answer 404 vs 412 rather than a vague 409. var current = await db.Pastes.AsNoTracking().FirstOrDefaultAsync(p => p.Slug == slug, cancellationToken); throw current is null ? new PasteRuleException("Paste was not found.", 404) : new PasteRuleException("The paste changed since you loaded it.", 412); }

items.title: Goal "rotation kills the old key; a rejected rotation changes nothing"
items.body:
Ticket 2 adds key rotation: send the current key and expected version, and a new key replaces the stored hash. The Goal has two halves, and the matching Check tests both. After a successful rotation, the **old key gets 404**, like the existing `AWrongEditKey_Returns404_SoAnAttackerLearnsNothing` test. A rotation sent with a **stale version gets 412** and the stored bytes are unchanged (`fixture.BytesAsync()`), like `AStaleVersion_IsRejectedWith412_AndWritesNothing`. All 14 existing cases must stay green.

Why the other Checks do not fit:
- the archive-then-repeat-create Check (assert 410) belongs to Ticket 3 (archival).
- the run-PasteCommandTests-against-SQLite Check belongs to Ticket 4 (move the store to SQLite).
- the pageSize query-string Check belongs to Ticket 1 (choose a page size).
None of them uses a rotated key.

excerpts.quote: **Ticket 2: rotate an edit key.** Add a command that requires the current key and expected paste version
After rotation, the old key gets 404, as in `AWrongEditKey_Returns404_SoAnAttackerLearnsNothing`.

items.title: Why the temporary file sits beside the workspace file
items.body:
To save, the store writes the new content to a temporary file, flushes it, then replaces the real file with it. If the temporary file were on a different drive (volume), "replace" would become a slow copy-then-delete, which can fail halfway and leave a truncated file. Putting it in the same directory keeps the replace a simple move on one volume. The guide: this "avoids a cross-volume move" and "reduces the risk of truncating the accepted JSON when writing fails". It is careful not to promise more: it "does not prove durability on every filesystem".

Why the others are wrong:
- Readers see the new content only after the replace, not before.
- The guide gives no reason about lease handles.
- The guide explicitly says it does *not* guarantee durability everywhere.

excerpts.quote: The store writes a unique temporary file in the active file's directory, flushes it, then replaces the destination. Keeping the temporary file beside the destination avoids a cross-volume move. This reduces the risk of truncating the accepted JSON when writing fails. It does not prove durability on every filesystem

items.title: What the utf8. plus base64url encoding of old keys is for
items.body:
HTTP headers cannot safely carry every character, such as spaces or Unicode. Older, user-chosen edit keys may contain these. So the client sends `utf8.` followed by the key's bytes in **base64url**, a text form that uses only header-safe characters. The server can decode it back to *exactly* the original key. The guide: "Base64url is reversible encoding", and "It does not encrypt that key." Anyone who sees the header can decode it, which is why a public service would still need HTTPS.

Why the others are wrong:
- Nothing is normalised; the original value is kept exactly, spaces included.
- Encoding is reversible, not one-way. (The server's hash is a separate step.)
- It is not encryption; the guide says a public service would need HTTPS.

excerpts.quote: Base64url is reversible encoding. For example, `utf8.` followed by encoded bytes lets an older key containing spaces or Unicode pass through an HTTP header without changing the original value. It does not encrypt that key.

items.title: Goal "the list request carries pageSize and resets to page 1"
items.body:
Ticket 1 adds a page-size selector (6, 12 or 24). The Goal is about the *list request*: it must include the chosen `pageSize`, and changing size must go back to page 1. The matching Check works at that boundary. The client tests (`node --test tests/client.test.js`) stay green plus a new test for the query string, and an xUnit case asserts that `pageSize=24` returns at most 24 items while `pageSize=51` returns 400. That 400 comes from the existing guard in `PasteCommands.cs` that allows page sizes 1 to 50, so the UI must never offer more.

Why the other Checks do not fit:
- the rotation Check (old key gets 404, stale version gets 412) belongs to Ticket 2 (rotate an edit key).
- the run-PasteCommandTests-against-SQLite Check belongs to Ticket 4 (move the store to SQLite).
- the user A's slug with user B's session Check belongs to Ticket 5 (accounts and ownership).
None of them sends a list request.

excerpts.quote: if (page is < 1 or > 10_000 || pageSize is < 1 or > 50) throw new PasteRuleException("Page must be 1 to 10,000 and page size must be 1 to 50.");
**Goal:** the list request carries the chosen `pageSize`, and the page resets to 1.

items.title: Why the edit-key receipt stays visible after creation
items.body:
The edit key is generated in the browser, and the server keeps only a hash of it. So the server cannot show you the key again later. If the paste was created but the browser lost the key (a closed tab, a crash), you would have a readable paste that nobody can ever edit or delete again. That is why the page keeps the receipt on screen, offers a download, and warns if you leave without saving it. The guide adds that copying to the clipboard is useful, but the app "does not assume that a clipboard copy is durable storage".

Why the others are wrong:
- The key grants editing; viewers of the paste do not get it.
- The server does not read a downloaded receipt back; the download is for you.
- The clipboard is explicitly *not* treated as durable storage.

excerpts.quote: The edit-key receipt is deliberately visible after creation. If a server accepted the paste but the client forgot the key, the user would have a readable paste with no way to prove edit authority. The page therefore lets the user download a receipt and warns about leaving an unsaved one. Copying the key is useful, but the application does not assume that a clipboard copy is durable storage.
The server stores a SHA-256 hash and compares supplied keys using a fixed-time comparison.

items.title: What protects creation receipts in SQLite when checks race
items.body:
Two requests with the same request ID can both run an application-level check ("is there already a receipt?"), both see "no", and both try to insert. A check in code cannot stop that race. A **UNIQUE** constraint on the request ID can: the database allows only one row with that ID, so the second insert fails. In the sketch's schema `RequestId` is the primary key, "UNIQUE by construction", and the comment says: "The UNIQUE constraint is the rule, not the code around it." The guide: "The database becomes the source of concurrency guarantees."

Why the others are wrong:
- The guide warns that keeping a process-wide lock "can hide whether your transaction design actually works".
- Comparing body hashes in C# is still a check in code that can race.
- Reading the table first is the same check-then-act pattern that races.

excerpts.quote: -- The idempotency receipt. The UNIQUE constraint is the rule, not the code around it. CREATE TABLE CreationRequests ( RequestId TEXT PRIMARY KEY, -- UNIQUE by construction
A unique request-ID constraint protects creation receipts even when application checks race. The database becomes the source of concurrency guarantees

items.title: Goal "archival never re-opens a retry window": which check fits
items.body:
Ticket 3 removes expired pastes from the active collection. The danger: if archival also deleted the creation **receipt**, an old create request retried later would find no receipt and create the paste again. The Goal says that must never happen. The matching Check keeps `DeletingAPaste_KeepsItsReceipt_SoAnOldCreateCannotResurrectIt` green and adds a sibling test: archive an expired paste, repeat its original create with the same request ID and payload, and assert **410** rather than a fresh paste. 410 comes from the branch in `PasteCommands.cs` that says the request "was already accepted, but its paste is deleted or expired. It was not created again."

Why the other Checks do not fit:
- the user A's slug with user B's session Check belongs to Ticket 5 (accounts and ownership).
- the run-PasteCommandTests-against-SQLite Check belongs to Ticket 4 (move the store to SQLite).
- the rotation Check (old key gets 404, stale version gets 412) belongs to Ticket 2 (rotate an edit key).

excerpts.quote: Add a sibling test: archive an expired paste, then repeat its original `CreateAsync` with the same request ID and payload, and assert 410 rather than a fresh paste.
if (existing is null || existing.IsExpired(now)) throw new PasteRuleException("This creation request was already accepted, but its paste is deleted or expired. It was not created again.", 410);

items.title: Goal "same contract against both stores": which check fits
items.body:
Ticket 4 replaces the JSON file store with SQLite while keeping the HTTP and UI behaviour. The Goal says the same *behavioural contract* must pass against both stores. The natural proof is to run the existing `PasteCommandTests` against the SQLite implementation **without editing a single assertion**: if the tests pass unchanged, the new store behaves like the old one. The Check also names the one test that cannot carry over (it locks the JSON file) and asks you to explain what replaces it.

Why the other Checks do not fit:
- the rotation Check (old key gets 404, stale version gets 412) belongs to Ticket 2 (rotate an edit key); it adds rotation tests, it does not compare two stores.
- the pageSize query-string Check belongs to Ticket 1 (choose a page size).
- the user A's slug with user B's session Check belongs to Ticket 5 (accounts and ownership).

excerpts.quote: **Ticket 4: move the store to SQLite.** Keep the HTTP and UI behavior while replacing the aggregate JSON implementation.
run `PasteCommandTests` against the SQLite implementation without editing a single assertion.

items.title: Why a file lease does not replace the version check
items.body:
The two mechanisms answer different questions. The **lease** makes each read-check-write sequence exclusive, so two processes take turns instead of interleaving. But taking turns does not stop a stale draft: if Tab B's draft is based on version 4, it can still run its turn after Tab A's and overwrite A's work. The **version check** is what notices that B's draft is out of date. The guide: "A lease alone merely serializes two overwrites; a version check outside the lease can race. Both checks must cover the actual persistence boundary."

Why the others are wrong:
- The guide says nothing about leases expiring mid-write.
- The version check has nothing to do with unblocking reads.
- The guide describes the lease as working among "cooperating processes"; it does not blame Windows.

excerpts.quote: A file lease and a version check are complementary. The lease makes each read-check-write sequence exclusive among cooperating processes. The version check determines whether a user's particular draft is based on the current record. A lease alone merely serializes two overwrites; a version check outside the lease can race. Both checks must cover the actual persistence boundary.

items.title: Start here: the paste workspace course and its order
items.body:
This pack uses a small pastebin: a React client and an ASP.NET Core API that store pastes in one bounded JSON "workspace" file on your machine. Each paste has an **edit key** that lets its holder change it. The course lives in `astraupskill/`.

Read in this order:

- **astraupskill/README.md**: what the course covers, prerequisites, a glossary and a time estimate.
- **01-CODEBASE-MAP.md**: where each part of a request is handled.
- **02-CONCEPTS.md**: the ideas the concept quizzes test: edit keys, idempotent retries, version checks, file leases, safe file replacement and limits.
- **03-WORKED-CHANGE.md**: one change made end to end (keeping a stale edit for review).
- **04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md**: how to run the tests and what each tier proves.
- **05-PRACTICE.md**: five practice tickets, each with a **Goal** and a **Check**. The goal-check quizzes come from here.
- **06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md**: solution sketches and a review rubric. Read it after trying the tickets.

Keep `backend/Domain/PasteCommands.cs` open: most rules end in one of its `PasteRuleException` lines.

excerpts.quote: This course follows the actual React and ASP.NET Core application in this folder.
Complete these on a disposable copy or branch.

items.title: What not to do when the receipt cap approaches
items.body:
The workspace has hard limits: 2,000 pastes, 10,000 receipts, 10,000 activity entries and 20 MiB. Receipts are what make create retries safe: a receipt lets the server recognise a repeated request and return the existing paste instead of making a duplicate. If you quietly deleted old receipts to stay under the cap, old retries could create duplicates again, with no error to tell anyone. The guide: "plan export, archival or a database migration rather than silently dropping receipts that prevent duplicate creations."

Why the other options are acceptable:
- Planning a database migration is one of the recommended paths.
- Exporting or archiving older data is also recommended.
- Refusing new writes with a clear error is not silent, so it does not lose protection without notice.

excerpts.quote: The limits are part of the design: at most 2,000 stored pastes, 10,000 receipts, 10,000 activity entries and a 20 MiB workspace. The store loads and rewrites the aggregate for each accepted mutation. That is understandable for a teaching application and unsuitable for unbounded traffic or history. When the cap approaches, plan export, archival or a database migration rather than silently dropping receipts that prevent duplicate creations.
